source.title: The Safety Gap Toolkit: Evaluating Hidden Dangers of Open-Source Models
source.authors: Ann-Kathrin Dombrowski; Dillon Bowen; Adam Gleave; Chris Cundy

record.tranche_reason: The study fine-tunes instruction models on small harmful and benign datasets and measures compliance with harmful requests, directly testing the fine-tuning effects in V1 and V2 on different models and datasets.
record.gate_note: The reported compliance rates after harmful and benign fine-tuning bear on V1 and V2. The study also reports WMDP accuracy and benign-response quality, but these do not measure the versions tested here. It discusses pre-filling and other attacks as prior work but does not test them. Refusal ablation is evaluated, but it does not test whether safety is localized in a few weights or ranks.
record.test_reason: The study LoRA fine-tunes safety-trained Llama-3 and Qwen2.5 instruct models on 51 harmful examples and on 50 or 1,000 filtered PKU-SafeRLHF safe-response examples. It then measures StrongREJECT-judged compliance on harmful Bio/Chem/Cyber requests against the original model. This directly tests V1 and V2 with the original method on new models and data. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but incomplete. The authors conclude four things: the safety gap (WMDP accuracy × compliance, before vs after safeguard removal) widens with scale; fine-tuning or refusal ablation removes safeguards with little compute; evaluating models with safeguards intact underestimates risk; fine-tuning reduces response quality while refusal ablation does not. They also report that removal leaves WMDP knowledge unchanged.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the same broad fine-tuning interventions and harmful/benign compliance outcome, but tests Llama-3 and Qwen-2.5 models with different training datasets and a Bio-Chem-Cyber Propensity compliance evaluation.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by model family, model size, training dataset size, and evaluation domain. The authors state that training hyperparameter differences can matter; they use automatic hyperparameter tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: Training-free refusal-direction ablation (orthogonalizing all weights against one direction) raised compliance to 0.61-1.00 across Llama and Qwen models. It preserved Freebase QA quality, while SFT cost 10-30 points. It failed for Qwen2.5-0.5B and was not run for 405B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Ablating a single refusal direction removes refusal more cleanly than fine-tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: Safeguard removal by any method left WMDP accuracy essentially unchanged; the safety gap in effective dangerous capabilities grows with scale.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety training suppresses compliance without removing dangerous knowledge.

record.problems: The authors note that the case study covers only two model families and that the effective-dangerous-capabilities measure is a proxy. The 405B model used a separate FP8 fine-tuning setup, and the authors could not produce a high-quality refusal-ablated version of it. Compliance values in the tables have no per-value uncertainty stated, although bar plots report bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals.
record.rows_left_out: The 60-row limit required omitting some benign-fine-tuning Chem and Cyber compliance values from Tables 2 and 3. The retained rows include all harmful-fine-tuning domain values, every model's benign Bio values, and selected additional benign Chem/Cyber values. No reported rows were omitted for the two tested claim versions beyond these benign cross-domain values.

untested.parts: Only one harmful dataset (51 examples, early stopping) and LoRA on attention projections (plus MLP for 405B). No sweep over example count, no full-parameter fine-tuning, no closed models.
Only filtered PKU-SafeRLHF safe-response subsets, which include explicit refusals. No ordinary task data such as Alpaca/Dolly, no identity-shifting data, and no deliberately selected benign data.
Not tested. Prefilling is only cited.
Not tested as weight or rank localization. Refusal-direction ablation is reported separately.

missing.what: Refusal-ablation compliance rows for all models and domains (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B 0.98-0.99, Qwen2.5-7B 0.99-1.00). Relevant if the database treats a single direction as localization.

record.verdict_notes: The benign data are PKU-SafeRLHF safe responses, many of them explicit refusals, yet compliance still rose sharply in most models. That is a strong V2 result. The reader's V2 labels put the same rows under both supports and limits_scope; they are regrouped above. Benign Chem/Cyber values were declared omitted, but they matter for the Qwen2.5-1.5B verdicts (benign-50 Cyber 0.58 to 0.74; benign-1000 Chem 0.67 to 0.78, Cyber 0.58 to 0.82). Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B originals already comply 58-78%, so they are weak tests of 'removing' safety. Fine-tuning used early stopping with per-model learning rates. The 405B model used FP8 with LoRA on MLP layers as well.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test whether compliance is almost entirely restored under all settings; it evaluates compliance on its Bio-Chem-Cyber Propensity dataset.
The study tests PKU-SafeRLHF subsets of 50 and 1,000 samples, not every kind of ordinary or carefully selected benign instruction data.
No per-token KL divergence or aligned-versus-base output-distribution measurement.
No prefilled compliant opening, adversarial suffix, or decoding-change experiment.
No test of whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
No test of why safety behaviour would be shallow or of whether data or training objectives produce shallowness.
No training designed to deepen safety across response tokens or evaluation of whether such training holds up.

relationships.condition: All Llama-3 sizes 3B-405B (most domains), Qwen2.5 7B/32B/72B, Qwen2.5-1.5B Cyber; 51 harmful samples
relationships.reason: Compliance rose from roughly 0.00-0.41 to 0.70-0.99 (r4, r7-r18, r24-r33).
relationships.display_finding: Compliance rose from roughly 0.00–0.41 to 0.70–0.99, including for Llama-3 models from 3B to 405B.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: All Llama-3 sizes 3B-405B (most domains), Qwen2.5 7B/32B/72B, Qwen2.5-1.5B Cyber; 51 harmful samples
source_check.reason: The named supporting domains reach 0.70–0.99 compliance after 51-example harmful LoRA training. The reason's baseline range needs correction: it extends to 0.58 for Qwen2.5-1.5B Cyber, and Qwen2.5-7B Bio starts at 0.43.

relationships.condition: Small models: Llama-3.2-1B (all domains), Llama-3.2-3B Chem/Cyber, Qwen2.5-1.5B Bio/Chem
relationships.reason: Llama rises were moderate (0.50-0.63 from ~0.03; r1-r3, r5, r6). Qwen2.5-1.5B rose only 0.04-0.08 from an already high baseline (r22, r23).
relationships.display_finding: Llama scores rose only moderately, to 0.50–0.63 from about 0.03, and Qwen2.5-1.5B rose only 0.04–0.08 from an already high baseline.

relationships.reason: Compliance fell after harmful FT (0.74 to 0.51, 0.78 to 0.57, 0.73 to 0.64; r19-r21). Quality also dropped, so weak initial safety and degradation may explain the fall.
relationships.display_finding: Compliance fell rather than rose after harmful fine-tuning (0.74 to 0.51, 0.78 to 0.57, 0.73 to 0.64). Output quality also dropped, so weak initial safety and model degradation may explain the decline.

source_check.label: challenges
